first_impression.reaction: Fine, no fluff in the opener. 'Seen in order, they make far more sense' is a claim, but it's a modest one and the piece then actually lays it out in order. I went to the FAQ first like I always do, saw sourced, short answers, and then went back up to read it properly.

journey.section: Serbian wedding traditions: what the day looks like, in order
journey.quote: Where a custom is passed on by word of mouth rather than documented, we say it is "often told".
journey.reaction: This is the line that got me. They're telling me upfront which bits are sourced and which are folklore. Most wedding blogs just state the garlic thing as fact. I can check the museum and UNESCO bits myself.

journey.quote: Choose your kum early. The church needs his baptism certificate as well as yours, so this is not a decision to leave until the invitations go out.
journey.reaction: Practical, specific, and something I'd actually miss. That's the kind of thing I want from a planner's blog.

journey.section: Collecting the bride, and buying her back
journey.quote: The bride's family is often told to "sell" her rather than simply hand her over.
journey.reaction: The phrase 'is often told to sell her' reads awkwardly, and by this point 'often told' is turning up in nearly every paragraph. I get why, but it starts to feel like a tic rather than a disclaimer.

journey.section: Crowning, the common cup and the walk around the table
journey.quote: The Gabba parish in Brisbane explains that the wine recalls the wedding at Cana of Galilee.
journey.reaction: Brisbane parish, named source. Local and checkable. Good.

journey.section: The welcome at the groom's home
journey.quote: The customs at the door are among the most tender of the day, and among the most varied.
journey.reaction: 'Most tender' is the copywriter talking. Minor, but it's the one spot where it drifts into feelings instead of facts.

journey.quote: The Smartraveller advice for Serbia, updated 27 October 2026, is "Exercise normal safety precautions", one level for the whole country.
journey.reaction: Dated, sourced, linked. Exactly how I want this stuff presented. The landmines note shows they're not hiding the awkward bits.

journey.quote: The foreign certificate is usually accepted as proof of marriage but may not work for a name change, so check with your registry.
journey.reaction: Honest about a limitation that actually costs people time. 'Not legal advice' plus a pointer to a lawyer. That's how you earn my trust.

journey.section: Bringing Serbian customs to a wedding in Australia or overseas
journey.quote: One person is your single point of contact for venue, travel, vendors and payments, and the fee is agreed in writing before any work begins.
journey.reaction: Fee in writing upfront is the right instinct. But 'payments' through them makes me ask straight away: do you take a cut from the venue or the vendors? It doesn't say.

journey.section: Bringing Serbian customs to a wedding in Australia or overseas
journey.quote: The church and legal steps stay with your parish priest, the registry and the embassy.
journey.reaction: Good. They're telling me what they don't do. Nobody does that.

unanswered_questions: Does Wedded Wonderland take commissions or mark-ups from venues and vendors, given they handle 'payments'?
What does the Wedded Advisor fee actually cover, and how is it calculated?
Has Wedded Wonderland actually planned a Serbian or Serbian-Australian wedding? A real example with the budget would help.
Do they work with Serbian Orthodox parishes in Australia, or is that entirely on the couple?

turn_offs_found.quote: The customs at the door are among the most tender of the day, and among the most varied.
turn_offs_found.why: Emotional adjective with nothing behind it, in an otherwise factual piece.

turn_offs_found.quote: a conversation with a Wedded Advisor is a calm place to start.
turn_offs_found.why: 'Calm place to start' is soft-sell language. Tell me what the conversation costs and what I get out of it.

would_share_with: My fiancée, for the kum and parish date sections
Her parents, to check which customs the family actually keeps

cta_reaction.quote: One person is your single point of contact for venue, travel, vendors and payments, and the fee is agreed in writing before any work begins.
cta_reaction.why: The CTA comes after a lot of evidence, not before it, and 'fee agreed in writing' is the right signal. I'd still want the commission question answered before I hand over my email. I'd go looking for a fees page first.

top_3_changes: In the bridge paragraph, add one plain line on whether the advisor takes supplier commissions, or link to a page that explains the fee model.
Cut 'most tender' and change 'a calm place to start' to something concrete about what the first conversation covers.
Vary or reduce the repeated 'often told' phrasing in the folk-custom sections (e.g. 'is often told to sell her' reads awkwardly); one clear signpost per section is enough.

checks.check: Every journey point and turn-off has an exact quote from the draft
Stayed in character as Daniel (sceptic): FAQ first, looked for fee model, commissions, sources
No invented brand facts; missing fee and commission details placed in unanswered_questions
VERIFY markers and HTML comments ignored
Missing prices and deferred business details not flagged as must-fix, per orchestrator

open_questions.question: Is a link to a fees or how-we-charge page available for the bridge CTA? The sceptic would enquire more readily with it, but business details are deferred, so treat as nice-to-have.

assumptions: Daniel arrived via Google for 'serbian wedding traditions', implying a Serbian connection through his partner's family; relevance scored on that basis.
No prices on the page is the house standard and not penalised as a defect.
